summary: This best current practice specifies tests to check whether independent implementations of a performance metric RFC agree, like an interoperability test for metrics. Results are gathered under the same conditions and compared statistically.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people measuring the same thing should get the same answer. This is the way to check that.

questions: what is ippm standard advancement testing
what is the anderson darling k sample test
how do you test a performance metric
subtitle: How to show that independent measurement tools read a performance-metric RFC the same way, using statistics instead of interoperability tests.

tldr.problem: Advancing a metric RFC along the Standards Track used to require interoperability proof, but measurement systems do not talk to each other, so wide deployment does not show they measure the metric the same way.
tldr.mechanism: Measure under identical network conditions with several independent implementations, check each against the metric specification, and compare their samples with the Anderson-Darling K-sample test at 95% confidence.
tldr.outcome: The test evaluates the metric RFC itself: if implementations disagree for lack of clarity, the text is revised. Results go in an implementation report that accompanies the advancement request.

today: RFC 6576 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 176) from March 2012. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Metrics Need Their Own Test
sections.content:
RFC 6410 says widespread deployment and use is enough to show interoperability for advancement to Internet Standard, replacing the earlier interoperability tests of RFC 2026 and RFC 5657. That works for protocols, but wide deployment of different measurement systems does not prove they measure a metric in a standard way.

For protocols, interoperability means implementations talk to each other. For IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) it is only meaningful for control protocols such as OWAMP and TWAMP. So RFC 6576 defines metric "interoperability" as measuring statistically equivalent results under the same network conditions.

The product of the process is information about the metric specification, not about the implementations: which definitions are clear and unambiguous, which are not, and which options nobody implemented and can be removed. The methods MAY also apply to metric RFCs outside the IPPM framework.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally you check two toys work together by plugging them in. Rulers do not plug into each other, so you check them by measuring the same thing and comparing the numbers.

sections.title: The Basic Idea
sections.content:
Before two implementations are compared, each is compared against the metric specification. Options the implementors chose have to be documented, and it is RECOMMENDED to use identical options for every test. Calibrations the metric standard specifies SHOULD be performed.

Two implementations measuring under the same conditions are treated as collecting separate samples from the same underlying process. The hypothesis is that the two samples do not show statistically different properties. RFC 2330 and RFC 2679 suggest a 95% confidence interval. That requires careful design:

  • Network conditions and paths MUST be identical to the largest possible degree, including stable and unambiguous routes.
  • Implementations SHOULD use identical options and parameters.
  • The sample size must be large enough, and the implementation with the lowest average packet rate sets the smallest interval that can be compared.
  • Repeat comparisons with several independent samples to avoid chance results.

Comparison is not based on individual singletons, because comparing two singletons fails more often than comparing samples.
sections.plainLanguage: To be fair, both kids measure the same table at the same time, with the same kind of ruler, and they do it more than once.

sections.title: Testing One Implementation
sections.content:
An implementation is compliant with a metric specification if it supports the requirements marked MUST and REQUIRED. The degree of compliance SHOULD be noted in the report. Supported options SHOULD also be documented, covering the singleton, sample and statistics definitions, timing and synchronization, and any other technical part relevant to implementation.

The goodness-of-fit test suggested is the Anderson-Darling K-sample test (ADK), where K is the number of samples. Results of a repeated test with a single implementation MUST pass an ADK test at 95% confidence. The conditions must be documented: the metric resolution at which the test was passed, the parameters changed by an impairment generator, and its settings. The minimum resolution in the reported results MUST be taken into account.
sections.plainLanguage: First each kid checks their own ruler against the rulebook, and measures the same thing twice to see if they get the same answer each time.

sections.title: Getting Identical Network Conditions
sections.content:
Live networks make identical conditions hard because of parallelism in devices and networks, such as load balancing. The RFC proposes tunneling to avoid parallel processing of different flows, plus several parallel probe flows to collect repeated data. The measurement load must not congest the access link or overload the implementation itself.

An IP-in-IP tunnel can keep different measurement streams from being split over Equal-Cost Multi-Path routes if all inner packets share one outer source and destination address and port numbers. It should also be easy to obtain, cheap to operate, reliable and free of extra cost. The setup used in a delay metric test carried several 802.1Q VLANs in an Ethernet-over-L2TPv3 tunnel in port mode. If tunneling is applied, two tunnels MUST carry all test traffic between the test site and remote site. Software-based L2TPv3 is not suitable because it can cause incalculable delay shifts.

Packet size SHOULD be small enough to avoid fragmentation by the added headers (22 bytes for Ethernet 802.1Q, 20 bytes for the outer IPv4 header, and L2TPv3 headers). Setting this up is not plug-and-play, and skilled networking engineers should be involved.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine two toy cars racing down a track. To make it fair, both must use the same lane. A tunnel is a way to force all the test packets down the same lane.

sections.title: Comparing Different Implementations
sections.content:
The same statistical test used for a single implementation is used across different implementations, and the smallest resolution at which they passed the ADK test must be documented. Cross-implementation precision may be lower than same-implementation precision. Testers SHOULD pick the same measurement configuration. If the test fails because the text is unclear or has several legitimate readings, the text should be changed and proposed for consensus.

A two-sample test can pass or fail by chance. The number of samples per implementation under identical conditions SHOULD be greater than 2, and at least 4 per implementation is RECOMMENDED. In a practical test, ADK passed with 4 samples even though a 2-sample test failed. Further guidance:

  • Compared samples must be captured in the same time interval.
  • For rates, use at least 5 singletons; for loss, an interval should contain at least five lost packets.
  • Use at least 100 singletons or samples per implementation, because ADK detects small differences and fails with very large data sets (RFC 2330 mentions 8192 measurements).
  • Samples MAY be calibrated by the difference of their averages, and any calibration MUST be documented.

For one-way delay, clock synchronization matters. Ideal endpoints use GPS or CDMA time sources or nearby NTP stratum 1 servers. Delay samples are recommended to be discarded if delay is finite in one direction only, or if the one-way sum differs from the round-trip time by more than an X% that the RFC leaves for further study.
sections.plainLanguage: One try could be luck, so you measure several times and compare. If the kids disagree, the problem might be unclear instructions, so you rewrite them.

sections.title: The Verification Process and Report
sections.content:
The IESG must be convinced that a metric specification is clearly written, that enough verified equivalent implementations exist, and that implemented options are documented. Each metric, statistic or option to be validated MUST be compared against a reference measurement or another implementation.

If implementations do not measure equivalently and measurement error does not explain it, the implementations and the definition text are audited. If the text lacked clarity, it is modified and proposed for consensus and possible advancement. Any recommendation for advancement MUST come with an implementation report.

The report MUST include at least: the metric and RFC compared, the measurement configuration, a full description of the measurement stream and DSCP, the duration and probe size with the confidence level, the statistical test results, lab conditions that allow reproduction, and documentation that helps improve the specification. If a different setup is chosen, differences in packet size, addresses and ports, IP options, DSCP, or sequential rather than simultaneous capture can falsify results.
sections.plainLanguage: At the end you write a report: what you measured, how, and what happened, so others can repeat it and decide whether the instructions are good.

sections.title: Setting an Equivalence Threshold
sections.content:
To set a maximum acceptable difference, each metric is tested by two or more implementations, and also twice at the same time by the same implementation using different address pairs. The same-implementation result bounds cross-implementation equivalence, which is useful for metrics like loss or duplication that do not give a continuous distribution.

The implementation with the largest difference in these homogeneous comparisons gives the lower bound on the equivalence threshold. The RFC states it as Maximum_Error = Same_Implementation_Error + Systematic_Error, where only the systematic error needs to be decided beforehand. Appendix B covers ways to run the ADK analysis, using the R statistical language and C++ code.
sections.plainLanguage: If the same kid gets slightly different answers twice, then two different kids will differ at least that much too. That gap sets how close is close enough.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says only that the memo does not raise any specific security issues. Its subject is a testing and reporting method, not a protocol that handles data from untrusted parties.

It does flag that test traffic must not harm the measurement itself: the load must not congest the access link or overload the implementation under test.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a how-to for fair measuring, and the RFC says it adds no special safety problems.
